turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Most of it made sense. One thing didn't — two buttons at the bottom. Went to the wrong one first. Darker one drew my eye. That wasn't the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy is misleading because the "Continue Shopping" button has high contrast (dark background), making it appear more important than the primary action.
B) The vertical placement is confusing because the secondary action ("Continue Shopping") appears above the primary action ("Place Order").
C) The grouping of elements is unclear because both buttons are presented in the same style and size, lacking a clear visual distinction between them.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
When does this kind of task typically come up for you? What kind of work situation usually brings you to a screen like this?
turns.a: Checkout flows. Group purchase, external deadline. No time for re-reading labels.

turns.q: When you noticed that dark "Continue Shopping" button, what specific detail about your current order status were you trying to confirm or verify from the layout?
turns.a: Team purchase. External deadline. I was coordinating — others depending on the outcome. Can't afford wrong turns.

turns.q: When you saw that dark "Continue Shopping" button, what specific information about your current order were you trying to locate or confirm in the surrounding layout?
turns.a: Complete the transaction. First attempt. No detours.

turns.q: If you could redesign that button's visual weight to better support your goal of finalizing the purchase, what specific change in contrast or placement would make the primary action unmistakable?
turns.a: Get to the confirmation page on the first action. No wrong destinations. One correct CTA, one confirmation.

turns.q: You mentioned the dark background makes it stand out too much; is that high contrast due to the solid fill color, or is it the size of the button relative to the primary action?
turns.a: Order confirmed. Right destination. No wrong page.

turns.q: Looking at the "Continue Shopping" button, is it the solid dark fill that makes it stand out too much, or is it the size of the element relative to the primary action?
turns.a: Wrong button dominated. 'Continue Shopping' had the weight. Eye went there, not 'Place Order.'
